title: Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function
text:
Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

Design systems thrive on consistency, so where does randomness fit in? Through playful demos of organic typography, bouncing letters, and splayed cards, Brecht De Ruyte shows how the new CSS `random()` function brings a little imperfection to the web without JavaScript libraries or preprocessor loops that generate hundreds of lines of static CSS.

text:
Stop Treating CSS Container Queries Like Traditional Media Queries

title: The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface
text:
The Death Of The Button: Why The Best Interface Is No Interface

The web is evolving beyond menus, forms, and endless clicks toward experiences shaped around human intent. For UX designers, understanding this shift means re-evaluating their role, moving from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.

title: Design v ADHD
text:
Design v ADHD

ADHD is a complex and common mental disorder which changes how the person processes information, behaves, and functions in society. Common recommendations for “ADHD-friendly design” include reducing clutter, avoiding distractions, and simplifying information architecture. I argue that these suggestions do not constitute “ADHD-friendly design”, and that the real solution is more sophisticated and challenging, if not impossible, to implement.

In 2014, Ethan Zuckerman, a renowned media scholar and Internet activist, apologised for his role in inventing the Internet’s most hated marketing tool: the pop-up ad.

All of us have screwed up situations in our lives so badly that we’ve been forced to explain our actions by reminding everyone of our good intentions. It’s obvious now that what we did was a fiasco, so let me remind you that what we wanted to do was something brave and noble.

In the late 1990s, Zuckerman led a team at tripod.com — a popular service which allowed users to launch their own websites for free. Zuckerman had tried countless ways to fund the growing business until concurring that the only way to keep the company afloat was to bring in advertisers. The format invented by his team — a pop-up ad — would not only boost tripod.com’s revenue but change the Internet once and for all.

With the advent of the pop-up ad came the boom of intrusive, aggressive, and persistent advertising. The industry has weaponised our lack of attention and filled every corner of the Internet with meaningless distractions and quick rewards. Pop-ups embodied everything wrong about the advertiser-centric approach: it appeared out of thin air and demanded attention like a capricious baby, no matter what was on the user’s mind or what they were occupied with. Pop-ups reduced users to targets for the omnipresent advertisers.

The Internet today is the realm of noise and chaos. Advertisers are more vicious than their predecessors, and ads themselves have transformed to appear more organic and blend into the content until it is impossible to tell them apart. Users continue to limp around this inaccessible desert, constantly bombarded with emails and notifications informing them of special offers, keeping them up to date with what their friends have been up to, and begging them to return for more mindless entertainment.

How does someone with an already disrupted attention span find the strength to concentrate when the entire world around them is vying for their attention? How do they make decisions, resist temptations, and struggle to conform in an environment that does not suit someone like them at all?

In this article, we will discuss people with ADHD, what it means to live with this condition, and why existing design frameworks for neurodivergent users address the wrong problem.

Understanding Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder

ADHD is a neurodevelopmental condition that affects a person’s ability to concentrate and control emotions and actions. Despite being commonly associated with hyperactivity (hence the name), there are several distinct types of ADHD: hyperactive and impulsive (rather self-descriptive), inattentive (characterised by distractibility and lack of attention), and combined (the most prevalent type); each manifesting differently in each individual patient. Most commonly, people (especially adults) with ADHD have problems concentrating on the task at hand, be it a work assignment or a lengthy conversation.

MRI studies of patients with ADHD show various dysfunctions in dopamine and noradrenaline transmissions. The disorder particularly impacts the prefrontal cortex, the area of the brain involved in regulating attention, motivation, and emotion, which in turn affects the patient’s ability to concentrate, control, and shift attention.

Children with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder show prominent abnormalities in the inferior PFC and its connections to striatal, cerebellar, and parietal regions.

ADHD is not curable but its symptoms can be reduced and managed. There are essentially two paths to regulating attention deficit: medication and therapy. Medication is commonly prescribed to children with ADHD to address the biological mechanisms of the disorder and regulate noradrenaline and dopamine transmission in the brain. Cognitive behavioural therapy is widely used to enable self-regulation and form coping strategies. This duality, however, is a mere reflection of a wider conversation around how ADHD should be viewed and addressed. Should we side with the biomedical discourse of ADHD and choose to view it primarily as a medical category, or should we focus on addressing the flaws in a system that punishes disobedience?

It is hard to deny that ADHD affects — at times, quite severely — the patient’s ability to exist and function within complex social structures that require discipline, obedience, and compliance. Children with ADHD achieve less in school than their peers and face a higher likelihood of engaging in criminal activities. ADHD is positively correlated with anxiety and depression. Adults with ADHD struggle with employment and marital problems. Suicide rates among both children and adults with attention deficit are higher on average than in the general population.

A popular interpretation of the positivist biomedical paradigm may suggest stimulants as the most appropriate answer to curbing “undesirable behaviour”. Medication’s proven ability to improve daily functioning benefits the patient as much as an institution that will gladly drug “children into docility…in the service of a tacit project of social control”. However, acknowledging that the system obsessed with producing identical, obedient workers has little tolerance for defiance does not require viewing stimulants as a tool for enforcing cooperation. Medication is not the only way to manage the symptoms of ADHD, and it is not always the most appropriate as similar, if not more powerful, effects can be achieved with individual and systemic tools.

A more balanced take suggests viewing ADHD as the product of a complex interaction between biological and social-environmental factors. It would recognise and address the biomedical mechanisms and create opportunities for people with ADHD to function, express themselves, and realise their potential in social scenarios. This take dismisses neither medication nor therapy: it views them as valid and effective tools in their own right, but offers a reframing of what is viewed as a problem in modern society.

Take, for instance, students with ADHD, who are talkative, distracted, hyperactive. Such students are only problematic if we choose to view them as such and refuse to make the necessary adjustments to leverage, not curb, their inattentiveness. A teacher who prioritises classroom discipline is a teacher who disregards the evidence that pupils with ADHD perform significantly better when given clear instructions and expectations. The teacher’s focus on obedience and order blinds them to a multitude of opportunities to maximise student performance without disrupting the learning process: for instance, by using pupils with ADHD as peer educators. By framing attention deficit as a condition associated with some deeply problematic, anti-social, disruptive behaviours, we unwittingly set pupils with ADHD up to fail in place of a far better simple solution:

Optimal pupil performance is associated with brevity and clarity of sequences of instruction, the accompaniment of verbal instructions with visual cues and the availability of resources that pupils can refer to for reminders of direction and expectations.

The same, of course, applies to other areas of life impacted by ADHD. Building sustainable relationships, pursuing meaningful careers, enjoying the simple joys of everyday living, demand adjustments — not only from the person with ADHD but from the system itself. Reasonable accommodations are not synonymous with special treatment: they are designed to empower people who are otherwise deprived of the opportunity to function in society, not to absolve them of the need to put in effort. Such accommodations create welcoming environments where people contribute to common goals in the ways that suit them best, and where their needs and challenges are acknowledged and addressed.

ADHD v Technology

The relationship between modern technology and ADHD is complex. On the one hand, smartphones, wearable devices, and other gadgets are becoming increasingly prominent in health management and emotional regulation, complementing therapeutic and medicinal treatments with handy personalised tools. To-do lists and AI chat-bots, remote symptom tracking and online testing — adults with ADHD have plenty to choose from depending on what they wish to achieve. In addition to that, the Internet has played a big role in raising awareness of ADHD and reducing stigma around the disorder. ADHD diagnoses have increased in recent years — which, considering that women are far more likely to remain undiagnosed than men, is a positive development. Technology makes it possible for people to discover ADHD, better understand its symptoms, exchange experiences, and receive treatment.

On the other hand, the digital world is a ruthless, fast-paced, overwhelming space that is neither welcoming nor kind to people with ADHD. The rates of “Internet addiction” (which stood at 14% of children and 20% of adolescents in 2006 and has since increased) are astronomical, and neurodivergent individuals who are known to have issues with substance abuse and addiction are among the groups most affected by the phenomenon. In people with ADHD, Internet addiction is positively correlated with inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity. Social media is especially harmful: engineered to maximise engagement, these platforms use all sorts of tools to make it nearly impossible to quit or even reduce screen time. Excessive use of social media in particular opens the door to a range of side effects, such as low self-esteem, feelings of inadequacy and underachievement, and increased social isolation.

However, it wouldn’t be fair to blame it all on social media alone. Most modern applications are designed for engagement and employ a wide range of tools to attract and retain users. One such tool is gamification — a popular technique that uses game mechanics in non-gaming settings to reward certain behaviours and entice continuous and regular use. As research demonstrates, rewards make even the most routine tasks far more exciting, allowing users to do chores, learn languages, and socialise with ease. For people with ADHD, however, gamification is a double-edged sword: while it certainly helps make learning more enjoyable, it also exacerbates ADHD symptoms. Instant gratification makes stimulation easy to achieve, forcing the user to seek more and turning mindful gamified experiences into never-ending quests for novelty. It is worth noting that because ADHD comprises at least two major domains — inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity — the same technology that severely influences one may have little impact on the other. For example, this 2026 study found a positive correlation between the use of short video platforms and inattention but not hyperactivity-impulsivity.

The digital age has revolutionised how we create, distribute, and consume knowledge, making it far more accessible and affordable than ever before. The influx of new information and the ever-increasing speed at which new content is produced have transformed the way we live, amplified our anxieties and feelings of overwhelm. The abundance of options has further contributed to turning attention into an especially scarce and valuable resource. Today’s digital world is a terrifying place that takes users’ time and mental wellness in exchange for occasional dopamine hits. It is not designed with the neurodivergent user in mind, but it profits from their struggles: from encouraging fast, mindless interactions to enabling impulsive decisions.

Wouldn’t it be great if we could do something about this?

Why designing for ADHD is so hard

When it comes to designing for users with ADHD, recommendations commonly include reducing cognitive load, avoiding distractions, and relieving users of the need to rely on memory — solid tips that are little more than general UX principles, adjusted ever so slightly for the neurodivergent audience. These principles cannot replace a comprehensive design framework. As a complex disorder, ADHD poses multiple challenges: from social disability and academic and occupational problems to physical and psychological issues and risky behaviours. To design for ADHD means to address all these challenges at a fundamental level and, importantly, to understand why addressing them is essential in the first place.

In the book “Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement”, Ashley Shew describes how most solutions are designed for people with disabilities but never with them: “[universal] design employs and imagines our bodies […] while rarely (if ever) simply asking us what we need”. What is worse, many of these solutions are built to correct or conceal disabilities rather than accommodate them. Our products, services, and environments are not simply built for the able-bodied — they force people with disabilities to adjust, to adopt particular ways of using and existing in them with the help of technology, to pretend that their disabilities are fixed or cured. Let’s medicate an inattentive student. Let’s use therapy to subdue them. Let’s agree on a design principle like “avoid clutter” in theory but allow a neurotypical middle manager to break it as they and their overlords please.

Take Bionic Reading — a method developed by Renato Casutt, a Swiss typographic designer, that emboldens the first letters of each word in a sentence to improve readability by guiding the reader’s eyes. Bionic fonts are sold for $79 per package of 10, and the company offers many other paid apps and products as well. Bionic Reading is a premium product with good advertising. It spread like wildfire in 2022, often positioned as the best possible solution for people with ADHD, dyslexia, and cognitive impairments.

Does Bionic Reading actually work? The company’s original testing method involving 12 participants (which, to the founder’s own admission, produced mixed results) does not withstand scrutiny. A real scientific test involving eye tracking on a large cohort of participants revealed that “the selective bolding of characters within words does not facilitate more efficient word identification or enhance overall reading performance in skilled adult readers”. Other tests show similar results. Bionic Reading claims that it keeps the reader’s mind focused, but in reality, it is a commercial product that tries to force a neurodivergent brain to act normally. As Daniel Lavelle at The Guardian asks: “Maybe having a wandering mind isn’t such a bad thing?” Would a better way to increase comprehension be to encourage neurodivergent people to read slowly?

So, what would it really take to design better products for people with ADHD? The process begins, unsurprisingly, with inclusion. A 2025 paper, “Towards Inclusive Guidelines for Web Design for Adults with ADHD”, describes co-designing such a framework with a panel of neurodivergent and neurotypical users. The recommendations produced by the panel varied from general UX tips (avoid complex menus, limit the number of options, keep navigation similar to other products) to ADHD-specific guidance:

  • Avoid stock photos and decorative illustrations;
  • Avoid components that may be confused with ads;
  • Restrict scrolling to vertical only;
  • Avoid non-standard hover effects and decorative animations;
  • Indicate external links and buttons.

The paper assessed these guidelines, by having two designers with ADHD put together a prototype. Nearly all suggestions yielded promising results: users with ADHD found it significantly easier to navigate the prototype designed according to these principles and discover relevant information. In the neurotypical cohort, the results were relatively moderate, although non-ADHD users, too, benefited from simplified navigation, clear information hierarchy, and other improvements. Interestingly, the only design choice that was not well received was to use the Bionic Reading method, which reportedly reduced readability in non-ADHD participants.

Does that mean that checking the boxes above will make your product ADHD-friendly?

The answer is no.

Although structured layouts and simplified navigation definitely make products easier to digest, and rewards and incentives indeed keep users with ADHD engaged, these principles alone do not amount to an ADHD-friendly framework. By narrowing the recommendations down to a short list of checkboxes, we design for people with ADHD instead of designing with them. We attempt to make them “normal” rather than empowering them to be themselves.

Product-focused approach addresses the wrong problem. It simultaneously sands down a square peg and turns a round hole into a rectangle: both parts somewhat fit one another, and everyone pretends that they are not deformed and misshapen. It does not dare to challenge the system that produces square pegs and round holes: its job is to mitigate the damage, not ask questions. Its job is to make a pop-up ad less annoying, not to find a sustainable alternative. It is to have a phone number people in wheelchairs can call for assistance instead of building accessible urban environment.

Meanwhile, designing with ADHD is the process of co-creation, of mutual learning and exchange between neurodivergent and neurotypical partners. It entails, first and foremost, transforming the environment in which the collaboration occurs. A design framework for ADHD must therefore go beyond product considerations to inform product creation itself: from establishing healthy routines and enabling productive collaboration and reflection to protecting critical decisions against corporate interference.

Under this framework, a product team could add rewards to encourage daily usage, but cannot leverage anxiety and the fear of missing out that such rewards can create. This framework would suggest the team to apply the same principles to their work as well: set short-term, achievable goals, engage and reward team members, and respect each other’s time, space, and ways of working. This framework would ensure that the product is co-designed with neurodivergent users, not tested against some vaguely defined criteria. This framework would never give rise to another pop-up ad.

Is it such a surprise that this framework does not exist?

Pop-up ads are dead. The disdain for them was so strong that by 2004, when 6.2% of all ads on the Web were pop-ups, at least 20% of all Internet users had a pop-up blocker installed. Advertisers and tech corporations they funded did not cave in until new and improved formats came along. Pop-ups did not die because the public hated them. They died because something better was on the horizon.

Pop-ups are dead, but their story, their demise, and their complicated legacy make me dread the future even more than I already do. Corporations wish to cultivate users who conform, consumers who neither demand systemic changes nor require small accommodations. In the absence of regulation and external pressure, what could possibly motivate tech giants to consider people with disabilities, let alone involve them in making important decisions?

Pop-ups are dead, but people who pushed them into existence remain in charge: not the Ethan Zuckermans who inadvertently created monsters but decision-makers who breathed life into these creatures and set them loose. So long as they remain in power, so long as growth takes priority over customer experience and care, there will be no room for human-centric thinking or accessibility. So long as they continue to reduce all users to identical numbers in a spreadsheet, any considerations that do not immediately translate into revenue will remain an afterthought, forever postponed, abandoned at the bottom of the backlog.

Two years ago, a young, moderately stressed-out PhD student wrote an article about pursuing a doctoral degree while living with ADHD. In that article, the author discussed the struggles that people with ADHD face in academia, how bureaucracy and formalities are designed, as if intentionally, to crush all hope and excitement in neurodivergent people, and how simple accommodations and small adjustments may significantly impact someone’s career. That student was optimistic about the future — his own as a neurodivergent researcher, his peers’, and the tech industry’s.

In the time since, he “toughened up”. He filled out countless ethics forms, amendment requests, and research milestone reports. He completed standardised tests, passed exams, and handed in assignments. He faced every deadline, every requirement, every expectation head-on. There was nothing that could alleviate the pressure. The system itself was not interested in changing, so he changed his ways of doing things. He succeeded at some (not all) endeavours, though in the process, lost his passion for many things he had once adored. He became timid, dull, complacent.

Back then, he was excited about things to come. Today, I no longer see him in the mirror.

What to read

  • HealthDirect. Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD).
  • ADDA. Types of ADHD in Adults: Understanding the Differences.
  • Paul Cooper, 2008. Like Alligators Bobbing for Poodles? A Critical Discussion of Education, ADHD and the Biopsychosocial Perspective.
  • Paul Cooper, Fintan O’Regan. Educating Children with AD/HD. A Teacher’s Manual.
  • Louise C. Druedahl & Sofia Kälvemark Sporrong, 2019. A Foucauldian perspective on treating ADHD with medicine.
  • Gyöngyi Fekete & Andrés Lucero, 2019. P(L)AY ATTENTION! Co-designing for and with Children with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
  • Ashley Shew, 2023. Against Technoableism: Rethinking Who Needs Improvement.
  • David Skidmore. Inclusion: The Dynamic of School Development.
  • Margaret D Weiss et al., 2011. The screens culture: impact on ADHD.
  • Linda Wheeler, 2010. Critique of the article by Visser and Jehan (2009): ‘ADHD: a scientific fact or a factual opinion? A critique of the veracity of Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder’

About the author

Kristian Mikhel is a PhD Candidate at the University of Tasmania, a product designer and a founder of Paper and Pain, a design agency for good, an accessibility advocate, and the author of the free newsletter, “The Accessibility Apprentice”.

Design v ADHD was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: AI doesn’t care about your job title
text:
AI doesn’t care about your job title

Exposure to artificial intelligence runs through the tasks you do each week, not the role on your badge. Here’s how to measure yours and lower the risk.

My mom doesn’t understand my job, and it isn’t her fault. The closest I’ve ever come to explaining it is “I design how it works,” which is true and tells her almost nothing about my day.

It also works best when I’m wearing a black turtleneck and holding an iPhone, channeling my inner Steve Jobs.

That’s the curse of knowledge, and I’ve never directly defined my role in many of the places I’ve worked. Over decades I’ve managed design, product management, and engineering, and more than once I started without a job description. It wasn’t about my job title, it was about judgement applied through my experience building software.

Artificial intelligence doesn’t care about your job title or mine. It’s probabilistically predicting an outcome without looking at your LinkedIn.

In GPTs are GPTs, published in 2023, researchers from OpenAI and the University of Pennsylvania scored occupations task by task. They estimated that 80% of U.S. workers could see at least a tenth of their tasks affected, and about 19% could see at least half.

Those averages hide what matters for one person. Your exposure depends on how much of your week can be specified briefly and checked quickly, and seniority protects you only when it changes that mix.

For her work, she’s not exposed even though she’s in the models. From Claude:

The main trace of Jean Neeman in the art world is a single, well-documented piece: a teapot titled “Tea on the Go,” made in 1994 by Jean Neeman (American, b. 1948) from silver, copper, brass, and cocobolo wood, measuring about 8.4 x 7.75 x 4.5 inches. That puts her work alongside some serious company.

She doesn’t have to measure her risk because she’s an artist. I measure mine all the time so I can add value that AI can’t add, and that’s judgement.

The five steps below show how to measure yours, each with a prompt to run in Claude.

List Your Actual Tasks

Start with a week, not a job description.

List everything you spent more than half an hour on: the usability readout, the stakeholder review, the status update nobody read. Note the hours, how often each task repeats, and who reviews the result.

Also leave room for the white space between tasks.

Unblocking a teammate, the quick answer that saves someone a day, the thinking before a hard review: none of it shows up in a job description or on a calendar. It also goes unseen when people judge what you do, whether that’s a manager at review time or a researcher scoring tasks for exposure.

It’s often where you absorb complexity that, as Tesler’s Law puts it, can be moved but never removed.

Write it down anyway.

For a checklist, O*NET OnLine, the Labor Department’s occupational database, lists 31 tasks for Web and Digital Interface Designers. In Putting Tasks to the Test: Human Capital, Job Tasks and Wages, a 2009 paper, economists David Autor and Michael Handel found that tasks vary substantially within occupations, enough to predict wage gaps among people who hold the same job.

In Toil and Technology, written for the International Monetary Fund in 2015, economist James Bessen showed how automated teller machines took over dispensing cash and taking deposits. The tellers needed to run an average urban branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so the jobs held.

The title stayed the same while the job underneath it was rebuilt.

My own title changed in March, from director to senior principal designer. Neither title would tell you which of my tasks a model can do, but my calendar would.

Try It in Claude

Run these prompts in one Claude conversation. The first one drafts your week from your role, so you correct a list instead of writing one, and you can check its tasks against O*NET OnLine.

To map my exposure to artificial intelligence, don’t read my calendar or connected accounts, or ask me to describe my week. If you don’t know my title, ask once. Name the O*NET occupation you matched, and say if you’re recalling its tasks from memory. Draft 15 to 20 tasks from it, plus the undocumented work between them, for a normal week. Give hours, frequency, and reviewer for each, marked as guesses. Then have me correct it, including whether I manage anyone.

Score Each Task’s Exposure

Difficulty is a poor guide to exposure. In a 2023 experiment for Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier, a team led by Fabrizio Dell’Acqua gave 758 Boston Consulting Group consultants realistic work.

With the model, they did far better on 18 tasks inside its abilities but were 19 percentage points less likely to get the right answer on one task outside them. Coauthor Ethan Mollick calls this the jagged frontier in Centaurs and Cyborgs on the Jagged Frontier: tasks that look equally hard can sit on opposite sides of an invisible wall.

Score each task with two questions instead. I call it the spec-and-check test.

  • Specify the result. Ask whether you could describe a finished version in two sentences that someone else could follow.
  • Check the output. Ask whether someone could confirm it’s right in less time than it took to make.
A task that’s quick to specify and quick to check is exposed, whatever your title says.

Twenty variations of an empty state pass both questions. Deciding which of three problems to fund this quarter fails both, and for now that decision stays yours.

Then weight the list by hours, because the Pareto Principle usually holds and a few tasks fill most of the week. A task that passes both and fills two days a week is where your risk sits.

When leadership reviews a pie chart of where a team’s hours go, you don’t want to be on the wrong side of it.

Passing the test means a model could do the task, not that one already does. In Labor market impacts of AI: A new measure and early evidence, from its own March 2026 usage data, Anthropic found Claude covering about 33% of computer and math tasks, against 94% rated feasible in GPTs are GPTs.

So the prompt below has Claude try one.

Try It in Claude

Paste this after the task table. It ends with Claude attempting your most exposed task, so you judge real output instead of a forecast.

Score each task in my table: could a finished version be described in two sentences, and checked faster than it took to make? Answer yes, partly, or no for each. Then say honestly if you could do each task today, fully, partly, or not yet, and why. Mark tasks with two yeses as exposed, sort by hours, and tell me what share of my week is exposed. Offer to try my top exposed task so I can judge it.

Check Your Career Stage

In the August 2026 revision of Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab found no economy-wide job displacement in payroll data. Employment for workers ages 22 to 25 in exposed occupations, though, sits 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, mostly because companies are hiring fewer young people.

Experienced workers show no comparable gap, and the authors call these early indicators, not proof of cause.

Entry-level work is often the most specified on a team, handed down with clear instructions and reviewed by someone senior, which is where a model does best. Experience protects through judgment and context that rarely fit in a two-sentence spec.

A senior title over a week of status decks is junior exposure with a bigger paycheck.

If you’re early in your career, ask to own one small decision from start to finish. If you’re senior, hand your juniors judgment calls along with tasks.

Management will also change because there will be smaller teams.

Melvin Conway observed in 1968 that organizations build systems that copy their communication structures, which I cover in Conway’s Law. My extension is that much of management exists to carry that communication, so a smaller team needs less of it. Four people share six possible pairs, while 10 people share 45.

The flattening predates these tools. For The Manager Mass Exodus: How SMBs Are Flattening the Org Chart, Gusto studied payroll at about 8,500 small and midsize businesses. The share of their workers who manage anyone fell from just under 25% in 2019 to about 15% by late 2024. If you manage, move your hours from relaying information toward the decisions and coaching a smaller team still needs.

Try It in Claude

This prompt compares your task list against your experience. Correct it if it gets your background wrong.

Based on my title and experience, split my tasks into entry-level work (well specified and reviewed by others) and judgment work only I can do. If you don’t know my years of experience, ask once. Give the share of hours in each and, if I manage, how much goes to relaying information. Name the knowledge I bring that you could supply without my judgment. Tell me plainly if my week looks junior for my title, and suggest one decision I could own this quarter.

Deepen Your Domain Expertise

Knowing your field pays off more than knowing your tools. For Agentic coding and persistent returns to expertise, published in June 2026, Anthropic studied about 400,000 Claude Code sessions.

People made about 70% of the planning decisions — that’s human agency — and the agent made about 80% of the execution decisions.

The researchers rated expertise task by task and said it differs from job title: a senior engineer asking a first question about the Rust language counts as a beginner at Rust. Expert sessions succeeded about twice as often as novice ones, and a working grasp of the domain captured most of that gain, the same early-steep curve as the Power Law of Practice.

The person who understands the problem and not the model gets more out than the person who understands the model and not the problem.

Knowledge on its own doesn’t protect you anymore: If what you know can be pulled from a large language model without judgment to apply it, you’re at risk.

Companies don’t need you to tell them something they already know, they need the person who knows which answer fits this customer and this quarter, and the person who acts as connective tissue between people, building trust and getting decisions made rather than relaying status.

If you’re neither, your expertise is a search ot an AI Assistant result.

For designers, the domain is the user’s world and the business around it. Get closer to your users’ domain than your product manager is: read the regulations your customers follow, sit with support for a day, and learn how the money moves.

Try It in Claude

Answer the way you would with a new manager, without polishing. Short, unsure answers show the gaps fastest.

If you don’t know what my company sells, ask once. Tell me in one sentence who my product serves, and let me correct it. Ask me eight to 10 questions, one at a time, about their regulations, money, metrics, and workflow; “not sure” is a fine answer. Rank my knowledge gaps by how much they’d change my design decisions, suggest one way to close the top gap in 30 days, and revise the decision you suggested earlier.

Rebuild Your Portfolio

Employers expect 39% of workers’ core skills to change by 2030, according to the World Economic Forum’s The Future of Jobs Report 2025. A portfolio of polished final screens puts the fastest-changing part of your job up front and hides the part that holds its value.

Rebuild it around decisions: the problem you chose and the ones you turned down, the tradeoff and why, and what happened after launch. Show one case where you directed a model, caught its mistake, and shipped the fix.

Show the work a model couldn’t have done without you.

Look sideways too.

O*NET lists 10 related occupations for the same designer category, from software developers to graphic designers, and jobs overlap where their tasks do. As I wrote in We’ve Seen This Movie Before: Desktop Publishing Already Showed Us How AI Prototyping Plays Out, typesetting effectively ended as a profession while graphic design grew into web, motion, and product design. They all adjusted, and we’re seeing this move now too.

Whole economies have also made this move before.

The agricultural revolution let fewer people grow more food, and the industrial revolution absorbed the workers it freed. In 1900, 41% of American workers farmed, and by 2000 fewer than 2% did, according to The 20th Century Transformation of U.S. Agriculture and Farm Policy from the USDA’s Economic Research Service.

The adjustment wasn’t gentle, though.

In Engels’ Pause, economic historian Robert Allen found that British wages stalled for roughly half a century in the early industrial era while output per worker kept climbing.

People adjusted, but it took a generation, and the ones who fared best moved toward the new work instead of waiting for it to reach them.

The good news is that employers now have software to map those overlaps, something Henry Ford never had. When Ford ended the Model T in 1927, about 60,000 workers were laid off, according to Last Day of Model T Production at Ford from HISTORY. Skills platforms such as Skills Cloud, from my employer Workday, now relate the skills across a workforce.

In the report’s workforce strategies chapter, 85% of employers plan to upskill and 51% plan to move staff into growing roles. Organizations are looking to reinvest and reinvent.

Intentions aren’t programs, though, as Dan Maccarone argues in What the AI era owes you for UX Collective Editors. You own your career, not your company.

It’s up to you to figure out where the hockey puck is going, the advice Wayne Gretzky got from his father, Walter, and your task list shows which way it’s moving.

Try It in Claude

Run this on your strongest case study first. Then reuse it on the rest, and keep the list of adjacent jobs it produces.

Ask me for my strongest case study. Rewrite it around my decisions: the problem, the options I turned down, the tradeoff, how I used and corrected artificial intelligence tools (or that I didn’t), and the outcome. Ask for missing facts one at a time instead of inventing them. Then list four or five jobs whose tasks overlap most with mine, what I’d need to add for each, and which carry more exposure than mine, using the earlier test.

Conclusion

The tellers’ story has a second chapter, and the branch boom that saved their jobs didn’t last. The Bureau of Labor Statistics outlook for Tellers projects employment falling 13% from 2025 to 2035, as mobile deposits and online banking keep customers away from the window. The first wave of automation changed what tellers did, and the second is taking away where they did it.That’s why the task list is a recurring exercise. Models improve unevenly, and a task that failed the spec-and-check test last spring can pass it next spring. Redo the list every six months and move a few more hours toward the work a model can’t finish without you.

There will always need to be a human in the loop, the person who commits to what the system proposes, as my Human-in-the-Loop entry puts it. Beyond that, there has to be human agency: someone who decides rather than someone who clicks approve.

My mom won’t be able to explain my job, whatever the next title is. A model won’t need the title to find my exposed work, and it can point out where it is.

Run the first prompt next Monday, before the next reorganization or the next model release decides the mix for you and how you can explain it to your mom.

Action items

  • Draft your task list. Run the first prompt and correct the table it builds from your role, or log every task longer than 30 minutes for five days by hand, using the O*NET task list for your occupation to catch what you missed.
  • Score each task. Mark whether a finished version can be specified in two sentences and checked faster than it was made, and treat tasks that pass both as your exposure.
  • Trade one hour. Each week, move an hour from your most exposed task to a planning decision, a stakeholder conversation, or time with users.
  • Rewrite one case study. Rebuild your strongest portfolio piece around the decisions you made, including any evaluation criteria you wrote and what happened after launch, and note which adjacent job its tasks would also qualify you for.

title: Human attention is the new old bottleneck. We have to design for it even more.
text:
Human attention is the new old bottleneck. We have to design for it even more.

Agents at Anthropic now log six hours for every human hour, and reading their output would eat half a week. The job is to create judgement systems for what deserves attention.

On October 16, four researchers at Anthropic published How employment is changing at Anthropic, a study of how its own agents changed the work.

Anthropic is one of the companies at the front of this shift, running its own work on the models it builds, so the study is an early read on where other companies are heading.

And honestly, it looks like previous studies in new clothing as I have linked below, just accelerated. Read on.

Here are the early results: By August 2026, agents directed by employees were logging six hours for every hour their people worked.

Agent sessions spent about 80% of their time idle, waiting for a person to answer. Even for employees who don’t write code, reading everything their agents produced would take more than half the workweek.

That’s the reading tax, and every team with agents will pay it.

None of this is new — we have decades of research and many, many principles like Automation Bias that we can apply to solve these problems. Now it’s up to us to apply them.

Underneath the numbers, the nature of work is changing yet again, and this time it’s turning everyone into a manager instead of a maker of widgets. That makes this a story about human in the loop and who keeps the agency. A person who can’t read what an agent did is still in the loop on paper, while the agent makes the calls.

That puts the problem on ground designers, product managers, and researchers already work.

Here are seven steps for keeping people in charge of that loop.

Measure Reading Time

Herbert Simon saw this coming in 1971. In Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World, he wrote that “a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention,” with most of the cost landing on whoever receives it. He meant data banks, and the line fits agents better.

Gloria Mark at UC Irvine has measured how thin it already is.

Her studies from 2016 to 2020 found people stayed on one screen for 47 seconds on average. Her first study, published in 2004, found two and a half minutes, according to the University of California’s How to sharpen your attention and meet your goals in 2024.

Every agent you add is a new sender in an inbox that was already overflowing with more information.

Anthropic measured the agent side the way a designer would, converting each session’s output into words read at 250 words a minute.

Even non-technical groups crossed half a workweek of reading.

Most days I build now, with a coding agent doing much of the work, and my limit is how much I can read and judge. So treat reading time like page load time, a budget a team sets and defends.

What’s lost in here is that a lot of work goes unreviewed, no human in the loop. Four hundred and twenty four hours is a lot more than the 168 a week currently has.

If one workflow’s weekly agent output, divided by 250, comes to more hours than anyone has, the workflow has a design problem.

Rank Agent Requests

One Anthropic engineer compared managing agents to babysitting. A child who needs a juice box opened and a child with a cut finger both arrive at full volume, and so do the agents.

Hospitals learned what that costs.

Joint Commission’s 2013 Sentinel Event Alert on medical device alarm safety estimated that 85% to 99% of alarm signals don’t require clinical intervention. Staff stop hearing them which is alarm fatigue in spades. Its database logged 80 alarm-related deaths between January 2009 and June 2012.

An agent that flags everything at the same volume has trained its human to ignore it.

Hospitals answered with alarm management: priorities, quiet defaults for routine readings, and a named person who responds. Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown at Xerox PARC described the goal in The Coming Age of Calm Technology in 1996, as technology that moves from the periphery of attention to the center and back.

Most agent interfaces skip the periphery and drop every request in the center.

Make agents justify a severity level for each request, keep the routine ones in the periphery as a digest, and bring only decisions a person must make to the center.

At Anthropic, agents mostly post in channels set aside for Claude-human work, which keeps the threads where people talk readable.

Design the Review Step

Review is where people pay the reading tax, and it’s where a human in the loop either keeps agency or hands it over. At Anthropic, agent-written code was removed or reverted at the same rates as code the same engineers wrote by hand, though the authors caution that agent errors may be harder to spot.

Perception is the bigger risk. In Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, a 2025 trial, METR found that 16 experienced developers took 19% longer with artificial intelligence tools after expecting to save 24%.

If people can’t tell how long review takes, they can’t tell when they’ve stopped doing it.

Andrej Karpathy made the same point in Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again), his June 2025 keynote for Y Combinator. Models generate and people verify, he said, so the loop between them should run as fast as possible, with the model kept “on the leash.”

My Automation Bias entry on UX Guidelines covers what happens when that cycle slackens: people approve what the machine proposes and miss what it never flagged.

A review screen should show what changed next to what existed, what the agent checked and skipped, and where each claim came from.

Put the riskiest change first, and log review time per item so the team can see the tax.

Write Decisions Down

A manager’s decisions only count if the agents can see them. Agents reason from whatever people leave in the open. One Anthropic employee’s name stayed on a months-old document about company swag, so agents kept sending them requests for T-shirts and mugs long after the job changed hands.

Shopify’s chief executive, Tobias Lütke, gave this work its popular name in June 2025. He preferred “context engineering” to prompt engineering and called it the core skill, as Simon Willison recorded in Context engineering.

Anthropic’s engineers add, in Effective context engineering for AI agents, that a model’s context is a finite attention budget. Every loop runs on two budgets, the agent’s context and the person’s reading time.

The cheapest way to protect a person’s attention is to write the decision down once, where every agent can find it.

At Anthropic, written standing instructions for agents grew from a few hundred to 8,500 in a year. Meeting time grew 20% for the median employee and agents see none of a meeting unless someone writes it up.

For design and research teams, this is familiar work. Decision logs, research repositories, and design rationale used to be documentation few people opened.

Now agents read every page, which raises the bar for keeping it current and owned.

Manage the Agents

At Anthropic, a fifth of employees surveyed in April 2026 said their role had shifted from doing the work to managing Claudes, and interviewees described individual contributors making VP-level decisions. Peter Drucker saw the first version of this in The Effective Executive in 1967, writing that “every knowledge worker in a modern organization is an ‘executive’” if they’re responsible for a contribution.

Agents extend that to anyone with a login, and Microsoft’s The 2025 Annual Work Trend Index: The Frontier Firm is born has a name for the role: agent boss.

I call it the work about the work, and the report calls the supporting work meta-work: specifications for multi-agent runs, loops where one agent reviews another, and pipeline dashboards.

It grew from 10% of employees’ interactive sessions in fall 2025 to 22% in spring 2026. Ethan Mollick argues in Management as AI superpower that this is ordinary management. What’s scarce, he writes, is “knowing what to ask for.”

Every one of those homemade dashboards is a product nobody designed.

Christopher Noessel argued for designing this layer in Designing Agentive Technology in 2017. Anthropic’s content team shows where it leads: the writers behind the greetings on Claude.ai taught agents to write that copy, then moved into writing prompts and evaluations.

Designers and researchers already have a manager’s skills here; the job is to claim this layer before it hardens into internal scripts.

Hire for Judgment

At Anthropic, an automated review of interview scorecards found that mentions of candidates’ creative use of artificial intelligence tools roughly tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for non-technical ones between 2024 and 2026. For technical candidates, comments on autonomy and judgment rose the most, while domain expertise shrank as a share of the assessment. In effect, Anthropic is hiring managers of agents.

Kent Beck, who created extreme programming, saw the split early. In April 2023 he wrote 90% of My Skills Are Now Worth $0, with a subtitle saying the other 10% were worth 1,000 times more.

A portfolio of polished screens shows what a model can now produce, and a record of what you rejected shows judgment.

The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025 found that seven in 10 employers consider analytical thinking a core skill, the top of its list. For anyone in design, research, or product, that changes what goes in a portfolio and what happens in an interview.

Show the decision trail: what the agent proposed, what you cut, and why the result held up with users.

In interviews, hand candidates a page of agent output with three planted problems, and watch which ones they catch first.

Rebuild Entry-Level Roles

The hardest number in the report concerns people never hired. Junior employees’ share of Anthropic’s technical departments slipped from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and junior technical hires fell from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic isn’t alone.

In Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence, Erik Brynjolfsson and two Stanford colleagues found a 13% relative decline in employment for 22- to 25-year-olds in the most exposed occupations. Not every executive agrees.

The Register’s AWS CEO says using AI to replace junior staff is ‘Dumbest thing I’ve ever heard’ covered Matt Garman’s argument from August 2025. Juniors cost the least and use the tools the most, he said, and without them nobody will have learned anything in 10 years.

The skill to supervise an agent comes from years of doing the work it now does.

Lisanne Bainbridge warned of this in Ironies of Automation in 1983: automate most of a job, and people keep its hardest part, the monitoring, without the practice that built their judgment. Entry-level roles in design and research can be rebuilt around review, with a junior making the first call on agent output and a senior explaining every override.

That’s an apprenticeship, and it costs less than hiring a senior who never had one.

Conclusion

In 1950, the United Auto Workers and General Motors signed a five-year contract that Fortune magazine called the Treaty of Detroit. Walter Reuther’s union gave management room to run the plants, and workers got cost-of-living raises, an annual wage increase, pensions, and health benefits.

The report reaches for that same settlement and names Anthropic’s version of it on three points:

  • Broad stock ownership
  • An early warning system for jobs at risk
  • A priority on moving people into new roles inside the company

Most of us don’t set compensation policy. We do set what agents show people, when they interrupt, and how review works. Those choices decide whether everyone’s new job as a manager comes with real agency or just a sign-off button.

Right now whoever builds the dashboard is making them, and designers, researchers, and product managers should be.

The study’s framing is careful. Anthropic is one unusual company, growing fast and building the models it uses, so its practices won’t transfer cleanly to anyone else. The direction is still clear enough to act on this quarter. Output keeps getting cheaper while human attention stays fixed, and the people who decide how it gets spent will shape what these teams become.

Action items

  • Measure one workflow. Count the words its agents hand a person in a week, divide by 250, and compare the hours with what anyone has.
  • Tier agent requests. Give every request a severity the agent must justify, batch the routine ones into a daily digest, and keep interruptions for decisions only a person can make.
  • Log decisions publicly. After any meeting that changes direction, post the decision and its owner where agents and colleagues both read.
  • Pair juniors on review. Let a junior make the first call on agent output, with a senior explaining every override.

Resources

  • Wilmers, Catipon, Massenkoff, and McCrory, How employment is changing at Anthropic, Anthropic, 2026
  • Herbert Simon, Designing Organizations for an Information-Rich World, 1971
  • University of California, How to sharpen your attention and meet your goals in 2024 (Gloria Mark’s research)
  • The Joint Commission, Sentinel Event Alert 50: Medical device alarm safety in hospitals, 2013
  • Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown, The Coming Age of Calm Technology, Xerox PARC, 1996
  • METR, Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity, 2025
  • Andrej Karpathy, Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again), Y Combinator, 2025
  • Patrick Neeman, Automation Bias, UX Guidelines
  • Simon Willison, Context engineering, 2025 (quoting Tobias Lütke)
  • Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents, 2025
  • Peter Drucker, The Effective Executive, 1967 (quoted from a Fast Company excerpt)
  • Microsoft, The 2025 Annual Work Trend Index: The Frontier Firm is born, 2025

Weekly curated resources for designers — thinkers and makers.

AI companies have spent the past year hiring forward-deployed engineers: engineers who sit inside a customer’s team, hear the problem firsthand, and ship against it. One count of 1,000 listings found the role grew 1,165% in a single year. This year I did a version of that job for my own newsroom, without the title, and it changed how I think about listening.

title: What if AI sets us free?
text:
What if AI sets us free?

What can destroy us can also save us. Here’s how I think we can stay in charge of the choice.

Casey Harrell is a climate activist. For years, ALS had been slowly taking his speech, until even the people closest to him struggled to understand what he was saying.

In July 2023, surgeons at UC Davis implanted tiny sensor arrays in the part of his brain that controls speech. AI learned to read the signals his brain sends when he tries to talk, turned them into words, and spoke those words aloud in a voice rebuilt from old recordings of him.

The first time he heard it, he said: “It feels a lot like me.” People who hadn’t heard his voice in a long time cried.

I’ve always believed that what can destroy us may also save us. Power can be wielded in many directions. It’s never just black and white.

Right now, most people who aren’t tech bros or tech sisses are either avoiding AI altogether or working from a narrow view of what’s actually happening (and what’s possible). Many are scared. The consensus seems to be: AI is coming for us, and that’s probably gonna make everything worse.

After a global pandemic and a fresh round of nuclear anxiety, AI feels like the next unprecedented thing. The one that might finally be the nail in humanity’s coffin.

But what if it’s not?

‘Good’ AI is a choice.

What intrigues me about AI is exactly this power: the potential for harm is enormous, which means the potential for good is too. Yin and yang.

So what if it all goes right?

Humans have always been driven by what if. It’s how we’ve crossed oceans, tamed fire, and ended up, well, here.

Exactly here. Collective anxiety, crisis, tech that seems to be racing away from us. It’s no coincidence.

But that potential. The opportunity. The blank canvas. The thrill of not knowing exactly what will come out of something is as scary as it is fascinating. And it’s what we’ve always been pushing towards.

This exciting sweet spot between what’s possible now and what it might make possible is what got me into designing products for a living.

And if that work has taught me one thing, it’s that technology is never neutral. Every product is a stack of decisions: who it serves, what it rewards, what it refuses to do. A feed that keeps you scrolling at 2 am is a design choice. So is a tool that hands you back your evening.

And the good AI stories, while harder to find in an endless feed of doom and gloom, are not lucky accidents. In every one of them, someone decided who it was for, put the right people in the room, and kept humans in charge.

Good is a choice someone made. What if we make more of those?

Yes.

What if?

What if it cures cancer?

AI is already catching cancer earlier.

Here in Sweden, Lund University ran the MASAI trial. Around 106,000 women in the Swedish screening programme were split in two: half had their mammograms read the traditional way, half with AI support. The AI group saw 29% more cancers detected. The final results showed 12% fewer cancers slipping through between screenings. Fewer of the aggressive kind, too.

As a carrier of the breast cancer gene, with at least one mammogram a year since I turned 30, I’ve spent nights worrying, not about my own risk, but about my daughters’. What if AI solves breast cancer?

Zoom out from one disease to all of biology. For 50 years, working out the 3D shape of a single protein could take a scientist years. In 2020, DeepMind’s AlphaFold learned to predict those shapes from a sequence alone. Two years later, its team released predicted structures for more than 200 million proteins. It has since been used by over three million researchers in more than 190 countries. The creators have won the Nobel Prize.

And then there are the superbugs. At MIT, researchers trained an AI to scan more than 100 million chemical compounds for ones that could kill bacteria. It found halicin, which killed strains resistant to every known antibiotic in lab tests, and later abaucin. Halicin is named after HAL, the murderous computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey. A reference to its significance.

The machine we were taught to fear is finding essential medicine.

What if interfaces fit every body and every mind?

For all of computing history, people have had to adapt to the machine.

AI is starting to flip that. Now.

Be My Eyes started in Denmark, founded by a blind furniture craftsman, as an app connecting blind people with sighted volunteers over video. In 2023, it added Be My AI: point your phone at a menu, a medicine label, or your outfit, and get a detailed description back.

Casey Harrell, whose story opened this piece, is the far end of the same idea: an interface that adapts so completely it meets you inside your own body — and maybe even mind.

So while most AI applications may feel like a boost for mass production, the opposite is also true. For the first time ever, we can create interfaces that shape themselves to us. Our eyes, our voices, our attention spans, our bad days. We can finally kill the norm and build custom at scale.

What if it gives artists better access to tools?

A friend told me about how low-income filmmakers in his community can now tell their stories due to accessible generative AI for film. And while “made without AI” is more meaningful, showcasing their storytelling skills may be the way to access funding that was limited to privileged groups.

I also see this in my life. It’s now easier for me to reformat my writing to make it easier to distribute, type off my handwriting to an online doc, and automate the organization layer of my creative process to allow me more time to actually create.

Last month I built an entire app to help me keep track of my ideas as voice notes. It auto-categorizes them and surfaces them back to me based on what I’m doing and where I am. It’s been a game changer for my process and one of the most fun things I’ve done lately: the app’s design is inspired by my kids’ squishy obsession, so the visuals and haptics are satisfying to watch, and tinkering with them was as fun as working on my usual pottery.

What if AI gives back to Earth?

Rainforest Connection hangs solar-powered listening devices in the canopy. AI listens for chainsaws, trucks and gunshots, and pings rangers’ phones the moment it hears one. The rangers from the Indigenous Tembé community use it to defend their land. The network now covers more than 736,000 hectares in 37 countries. What if we can protect the Earth before it’s too late?

Floods affect around 250 million people a year. Google’s Flood Hub uses AI to forecast river floods up to seven days ahead, even where there are no river gauges, and now covers places where 700 million people live, in over 100 countries. Google says flood forecasting in Africa is now on par with Europe. I can imagine there’s even more tech that can do to protect us.

There’s more to planet Earth than nature, so…

What if it helps unite us, humans?

In 2024, DeepMind researchers built an AI mediator, named the Habermas Machine (after one of my favorite German philosophers), and tested it with more than 5,000 people debating divisive issues. People preferred its summaries to a human mediator’s, groups moved closer together, and it worked minority objections into the final conclusion so everyone felt heard. The team behind it trained Habermas to mediate, not to persuade. The job was to find where people already agreed and write it down. If you think about it, it’s the same kind of technology behind the outrage engine of our feeds, just pointed the other way.

Could something like this eventually bring us closer together? Make us comfortable discussing and disagreeing again, so we can move toward a compromise and away from extremes and isolation?

AI as a peacekeeper. A tempting thought. A machine that helps us hear each other might be a step in the right direction.

What if it doesn’t take our jobs?

For most, this is the scariest part.

And yes, jobs will disappear. The World Economic Forum’s Future of Jobs Report 2025, based on more than 1,000 employers, expects 92 million jobs to be displaced by 2030 and 170 million new ones created, a net gain of 78 million. The fastest growth is expected in frontline human work like care and education.

Forecasts are guesses, though. And even if you believe this optimistic prediction, a net gain is no comfort if the job lost is yours — or if your next one might only be available after years of retraining.

I think the truth is somewhere in the middle.

In 2024, Klarna announced that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 customer service agents and handling two-thirds of its customer chats. About a year later, its CEO said the quality had suffered, and the company started hiring humans again.

What I’m trying to get at is this:

AI built to replace people tends to make things worse. AI built to support people tends to make things better.

MASAI didn’t fire radiologists; it gave them back 44% of their reading time. Casey Harrell didn’t need a new voice; he needed his own.

Whether AI takes our jobs or transforms them isn’t decided by the technology. It’s decided by people in meeting rooms, choosing what to automate and what to protect. Some of those people are designers. I’m one of them.

Most of those people do care.

I choose to believe that they, like me, take their responsibility personally and seriously. And that we can and will figure out a way to make AI work for good.

What if it actually frees up our time?

Last week, my friends over at Sanna, a Norwegian AI-accounting startup, announced that they were introducing a 4-day work week for their accountants.

In 2019, Finland’s then-future prime minister asked on a party panel why a four-day week or a six-hour day couldn’t be the next step, and whether eight hours was really the ultimate truth. It never became Finnish policy, but the question stuck. And we now know the answer can be yes. In the UK’s 2022 pilot, 61 companies cut hours with no cut in pay. Revenue held steady, resignations fell by 57%, and 56 of the 61 kept the shorter week.

I am hopeful that AI will finally be the technology that doesn’t turn efficiency into more work — because now the gains are so obvious, why would we not spend them on leisure, self-fulfillment, being with each other? Not doing that feels insane to me. I’m sure I’m not the only one.

I can imagine it.

A Friday that belongs to me: reading, writing, hanging with my kids, or maybe doing nothing at all. The stuff of Renaissance paintings. And maybe our future?

What if it takes us offline?

This is my most hopeful what if.

Almost every example in this piece still happens on a screen. That’s where we are. Right now. But I don’t think it’s where we’re headed. Screens add a digital layer to life that takes away from our lived experience.

I’ve always thought screens were never the point. I’m almost sure you’d agree.

We stare at our phones because that’s where the doing happens: the booking, the paying, the replying, the finding. Endless apps, each built to keep us locked in. If AI can do the doing, the reason to stare goes away. You say what you need, and get on with your day. And even further: what if you don’t have to be proactive at all; it can organize based on what it learns about you. The interface becomes secondary. Maybe, it goes away.

Think back to Be My AI. A blind user points a phone at a menu, hears what’s on it, and puts the phone back in her pocket. Think of Casey Harrell, speaking with no screen at all. The most advanced interfaces are already the ones that disappear.

Wouldn’t it be funny if AI is what finally breaks our phone addictions?

And there’s another argument.

When content becomes infinite and basically free, it stops being worth much. One-to-infinite, the logic of the feed, gets flooded with sameness. And when everything is generic, what becomes valuable again is the specific: the handmade, the local, the person who actually knows you, the things you can touch. With your heart, mind, and soul.

One-to-one, not one-to-infinite (I wrote about this before, here).

What if AI pushes our tech obsession so far that it solves it? It runs itself in the background. And we just do us.

Humans, human to human, together.

Don’t dream it, be it.

None of my musings cancel the risks. AI can (and already is) be(ing) used to surveil, manipulate, replace, and harm, and people far more qualified than me are right to sound the alarm.

But — I hope this came across in my piece — there is as much potential for good as for evil. Yin and Yang.

The future isn’t something that happens to us.

It’s something we build. And we can only build toward what we can imagine. If the only story we tell about AI is the one where it ends us, we leave the steering wheel to the people who don’t mind that ending. It’s their greatest weapon: to make us feel defeated, choiceless, numb.

So this is for the people who make things.

The designers, the writers, the engineers, the product people, the ones in the meeting rooms. We are the ones deciding, one screen, one button, one sentence at a time, what this technology rewards and what it refuses to do.

Ask who it’s for.

Put the right people in the room.

Keep humans in charge. MASAI kept a radiologist in the loop; Rainforest Connection put the tool in the hands of the Tembé rangers rather than a central authority.

Let’s build the version you’d want your mother to use at 3 am or your daughter to carry in 20 years.

And for everyone else: stay curious. Look past the headlines. Ask for the good version. Demand it. Stray from your feed. Occasionally, turn off the news.

Who knows what will happen? What can destroy us may also save us. Believing it might save us is our only chance.

So: what if it all goes right?

What if, one day, we look at the world we built with it, and say what Casey Harrell said when he heard himself again?

It feels a lot like us.

Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.
